sections.heading: Confessing self-centered service
sections.text: Lord, forgive me for the ways I turn service for you into service for myself. I have leaned on my own strength and gifting. I have pushed myself as if everything depended on me. I have enjoyed being noticed and praised. I have treated spiritual feelings as if they were proof that my heart was right. I have even trusted the strength of my faith instead of resting on Christ himself. Whenever I build on anything besides you, I am trusting flesh as my arm.
theological_themes: Repentance for corrupt motives in ministry
The danger of self-reliance in Christian service
Resting on Christ rather than on the strength of one's own faith

scripture_references.connection: This passage contrasts trusting in human strength with trusting in the Lord. It directly grounds the prayer’s confession that self-reliant service is a form of making flesh one’s arm.
Jesus warns against doing righteous acts in order to be seen by others. That speaks to the temptation to receive applause and turn service into self-display.
Paul says his confidence and competence for ministry come from God, not from himself. This supports the prayer’s rejection of personal ability as the foundation of service.

sections.heading: Learning what real faith does
sections.text: Teach me that living service does not come from pressure, image management, or confidence in myself. Faith awakened by your grace is what makes obedience real. It draws me nearer to you and lifts me out of myself, so that I am not merely running on natural ability. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, you are enough. You work through your commands and promises, and you also work quietly and powerfully in the depths of the soul in ways I cannot manufacture or control.
theological_themes: Faith as a gift of grace that produces true obedience
God’s all-sufficiency as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit
God working both through his revealed Word and by his inward power

scripture_references.connection: Paul ties faith, grace, and good works together: salvation is God’s gift, and believers are created in Christ for the good works God prepares. This supports the prayer’s claim that grace-stirred faith produces true service.

This passage holds together human obedience and God’s active work within believers. It fits the prayer’s request to serve while recognizing that God supplies the will and power behind faithful action.

sections.heading: Having no foundation but Christ
sections.text: If I do not have this kind of faith, all my activity is empty. My grip on you is not the foundation; you are. Keep my eyes on Christ, not on how strongly I think I am holding on to him. Show me your will through your Word, and give me the power to do what you command.
theological_themes: Christ alone as the foundation of faith and service
The emptiness of religious activity apart from dependence on God
Obedience empowered by God rather than self-confidence

scripture_references.connection: Paul says no foundation can be laid other than Jesus Christ. This directly supports the prayer’s rejection of any alternate ground for confidence in service.

Jesus teaches that fruitfulness depends on abiding in him and that apart from him his disciples can do nothing. This illuminates the prayer’s insistence that ministry without true dependence on Christ is empty.

sections.heading: Putting you above myself
sections.text: It is right for me to set you above everyone and everything in my thoughts, desires, and choices. But my sin is that I put myself above you. When I break your law, I am not merely making a mistake; I am treating your glory as less important than what I want. I choose approval, comfort, control, success, or some other created thing over you. Lord, show me how serious that is.
theological_themes: Sin as personal offense against God, not merely rule-breaking
Idolatry as preferring created things over God
The duty to honor God above self

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes sin as a refusal to honor God rightly and an exchange of God’s glory for created things. This strongly supports the prayer’s view that disobedience involves preferring something else to God.
David recognizes that his sin is ultimately against God. This helps ground the prayer’s emphasis that every breach of God’s law is personal before him, not merely external failure.

sections.heading: Serving by grace and love
sections.text: Help me hate the self-exalting part of me because it competes with you. Do not leave me curved in on myself. Keep me in the faith that works through love. Let my service come from grace, depend on grace, and give the credit back to you.
theological_themes: Service empowered by grace and aimed at God’s glory

scripture_references.connection: Paul says what counts in Christ is faith working through love. This directly supports the prayer’s final request for a faith that does not remain abstract but serves in love.

Peter tells believers to serve with the strength God supplies so that God is glorified through Jesus Christ. This matches the prayer’s desire for service that depends on grace and returns glory to God.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s phrase about faith resting on “my hold on Christ” is pastorally delicate. I rendered it as rejecting confidence in the strength of one’s own faith, while preserving the positive call to rest on Christ himself.

The original asks God to help the speaker “abhor myself in comparison of thee.” I avoided language that could sound like generalized self-hatred and expressed it as hatred of the self-exalting, God-competing part of the heart, while retaining the original’s strong humility before God.

The claim that every breach of God’s law arises from contempt of God’s person is a strong Puritan account of sin. I preserved its force by describing sin as treating God’s glory as less important than one’s own desires, rather than reducing sin to mistakes or weakness.
significant_interpretive_choices: I interpreted the original’s distinction between God working “mediately” and “immediately” as God working through his commands and promises in Scripture, and also inwardly by his own power in the soul.
I kept the explicitly Trinitarian address in the section on God’s all-sufficiency, since the original names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as the God in whom faith centers.
I rendered the prayer’s ministry language broadly as Christian service, since the original can apply both to formal ministry and to any act of serving God.
